title_en: There's a new Apple Music logo and it looks like ripples in water
title_fa: There's a new Apple Music logo and it looks like ripples in water
excerpt_en: Maybe they should use it as the app logo instead.
excerpt_fa: Maybe they should use it as the app logo instead.
content_en:
There's a new Apple Music logo and it looks like ripples in water
This should pair well with the Liquid Glass design language.
Apple just revealed a fairly unique design language and logo for Apple Music. It looks like a musical note floating underneath rippling waves, which should pair well with the Liquid Glass software interface.
The company says it was made via practical effects by etching the logo on the glass floor of a small tank. This tank was then filled with mineral oil and a transparent cover was placed over the logo. Next, Apple used an instrument to play a short series of tones, which caused the oil to ripple. They filmed everything and, well, here we are.
This project was a collaboration between Apple, music producer Fred Again and a company called NEST Acoustics. "For the rebrand of Apple Music, we wanted sound to create the visuals," a narrator says in an introduction video. "How do we take this idea of music and distill it into something visually beautiful? Essentially the idea was to create the perfect sound wave."
Apple has updated the Apple Music app icon in beta 4 pic.twitter.com/hcx1fknpGr
— Andreas Storm (@avstorm) October 13, 2026
The motion-filled rippling logo will be used at the beginning of Apple Music videos and stuff like concert footage. The actual app icon is going from red to black-and-white, which has not been a hit with folks on the internet. All of these changes are coming with the company's next software releases, including iOS 27.2 and macOS 27.2.

title_en: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C
title_fa: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C
excerpt_en: Blacksmith, a platform that lets companies build and test AI code more effectively, just announced a $66 million Series C round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
excerpt_fa: Blacksmith, a platform that lets companies build and test AI code more effectively, just announced a $66 million Series C round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
content_en:
Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.
“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.
The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.
The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

title_en: Waymo starts offering rides at the Las Vegas airport
title_fa: Waymo starts offering rides at the Las Vegas airport
excerpt_en: Waymo only just started offering rides to the public in Las Vegas in September but is already serving a 24-square-mile area in the city.
excerpt_fa: Waymo only just started offering rides to the public in Las Vegas in September but is already serving a 24-square-mile area in the city.
content_en:
Waymo is now shuttling customers to and from the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, with pickups and drop-offs happening at dedicated “autonomous vehicle zones” at Terminal 1 and Terminal 3, the company announced Wednesday.
This is the sixth major airport that Waymo is serving. The company already offers rides at Phoenix Sky Harbor, Nashville International, San Antonio International, San Francisco International, and San José International airports.
Waymo only just started offering rides to the public in Las Vegas in September but is already serving a 24-square-mile area in the city. The company said the rides to and from the Las Vegas airport will be limited at first to just a few riders, before opening up to all customers.
Amazon-owned Zoox already offers rides at the Vegas airport, and more robotaxis are coming to Sin City. In August, state regulators approved permits that will allow Tesla and Uber to put thousands of them on the city’s streets in the next year.

title_en: Sony's PlayStation Pulse headset arrives on November 19 for $100
title_fa: Sony's PlayStation Pulse headset arrives on November 19 for $100
excerpt_en: Pre-orders open on October 29.
excerpt_fa: Pre-orders open on October 29.
content_en:
Sony's PlayStation Pulse headset arrives on November 19 for $100
Pre-orders open on October 29.
Sony has revealed when you can get your hands on its PlayStation Pulse wireless headset. The cans will ship on November 19 in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and more than a dozen other countries. Pre-orders open on October 29. Availability in other countries will be announced later.
The headset, which is available in white and midnight black, costs $100. That seems fairly reasonable at a time when pretty much everything is getting more expensive. It costs $50 less than the PlayStation Pulse Elite, Sony's first planar magnetic headset.
The PlayStation Pulse has larger planar magnetic drivers than those found on the previous model. Sony says this allows the headset to deliver "fuller, deeper bass, while keeping the clean sounds players have enjoyed from Pulse Elite." The company added that the spatial accuracy offered by the drivers helps folks pick up on directional cues while playing games. The mic, meanwhile, has "AI-enhanced noise rejection" to minimize background sounds.
The headset offers Bluetooth connectivity as well as the PlayStation Link protocol, which connects it to supported devices such as the PS5, PlayStation Portal, Mac and PC. The tech is said to offer seamless switching between connected devices and lossless, ultra-low latency audio.
A higher-end model called the Pulse Edge is set to arrive in 2027. Sony will start shipping its $220 Pulse Elevate wireless speakers, which also have planar magnetic drivers, next month.

title_en: Supernatural's VR exercise app has relaunched on Meta VR headsets
title_fa: Supernatural's VR exercise app has relaunched on Meta VR headsets
excerpt_en: It's in early access and subscriptions cost $20 per month or $200 each year.
excerpt_fa: It's in early access and subscriptions cost $20 per month or $200 each year.
content_en:
Supernatural's VR exercise app has relaunched on Meta VR headsets
It's in early access and subscriptions cost $20 per month or $200 each year.
The VR fitness app Supernatural has returned to Meta headsets as an early access release. This is welcome news for fans of the platform, as Meta paused new content for the exercise app earlier this year. It has relaunched as an independent entity.
The new Supernatural costs $20 per month or $200 a year, which was the original subscription price when the software first launched back in 2020. The team promises new workouts every week, with many "back-catalog favorites" returning in the "weeks and months ahead." The first batch of new workouts arrives at the end of the month.
"It's not every day you get to make a comeback, but thanks to the Supernatural community, that's exactly what we're doing," said CEO James Senior.
The early access release already features thousands of workouts, including a bunch of remastered favorites. There are hundreds of music tracks to choose from and a brand-new virtual environment based on a glacial lake. Up to four people in a single household can share a headset, which should lead to some friendly competition. Returning members also can transfer pre-existing points, badges and fitness streaks.
The company is working on rebuilding the real-time workout platform, which lets people exercise with friends online. That won't be available for a while, as it's currently in a testing phase. It's also making a mobile companion app that tracks fitness progress. Finally, there will be even more virtual environments added to the lineup in the coming weeks.
Supernatural and Beat Saber were pretty much the killer apps for VR in the early 2020s. It's good to see they are both still going strong.

title_en: Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hands-on: Triple 200-megapixel cameras but few surprises
title_fa: Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hands-on: Triple 200-megapixel cameras but few surprises
excerpt_en: Trying to fill a OnePlus-shaped hole, Oppo plays it a little safe.
excerpt_fa: Trying to fill a OnePlus-shaped hole, Oppo plays it a little safe.
content_en:
Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hands-on: Triple 200-megapixel cameras but few surprises
Trying to fill a OnePlus-shaped hole, Oppo plays it a little safe.
Oppo returns with another flagship phone with telephoto accessories and impressive specs. The Find X10 Pro Max is launching across Europe, Asia and other territories, supplanting last year's Find X9 Pro and sitting below the Find X9 Ultra. However, if you're based in the US, it will once again be hard to get the company's newest phone.
Oppo isn't breaking much new ground this year with its upper-midrange Find X10 series. Those changes include some minor design tweaks. Aside from a standalone color sensor and flash positioned next to the camera unit, it looks like another Find X series 'pro' phone. The company seems to have kept the Find X10 design separate from last year's Ultra and Find N6 foldable with its circular camera design. A slender orange accent outlines the camera array, the latest nod to Oppo's collaboration with Hasselblad.
The materials and finish are further refined, with a matte-finish aluminum frame and a textured back panel that's actually quite smooth. (I thought it would be grippier!) The mid-flagship comes in Luna White (the phone I tested) and Titanium Grey, which has a smooth back cover that lacks the aforementioned textured panel.
The Find X10 Pro Max has a 6.78-inch display, roughly the same as the X9 Ultra, peaking at 3,600 nits. It's noticeably brighter than the Find X9 Pro. It also supports adaptive refresh rates from 1 to 144Hz, plus 10-bit color depth and Dolby Vision.
Oppo is keen to highlight the refinements it made to color temperature adjustments on the display, with faster changes in ambient light levels and a new "adaptive tone" option that uses a new five-channel sensor to better match the surrounding light. I couldn't particularly discern the difference in color changes. Still, auto-brightness seemed snappier when switching between dark rooms and bright outdoor daylight, which is crucial when trying to grab quick shots of a drone I was also testing at the time.
Cameras are still Oppo's smartphone obsession, though it gets a little confusing this time around. Its newest smartphone's cameras arguably aren't quite as potent as the company's flagship, the Find X9 Ultra, which launched only a few months ago.
That all comes down to the sensors. The Find X10 Pro Max comes with three (different) 200-megapixel sensors on the main, telephoto and ultrawide cameras. However, the Find X9 Ultra featured a significantly larger 1/1.12-inch main camera sensor from Sony. Meanwhile, the Find X10 Pro Max shifted to a 1/1.3-inch Samsung HPC sensor, making the X9 Ultra's main sensor roughly 25 percent larger. When I compared the phones' images, the X9 Ultra handled low light better, especially in Hasselblad Master mode, which strips away computational photography augmentations.
On that note, there's also a new "Lumo True" image engine for natural color, tones and textures, which minimizes aggressive AI processing, and that bears out. Compared with the X9 Pro and Ultra, the X10 Pro Max makes fewer computational guesses on text detail and patterning from excessive AI correction.
The Find X10 Pro Max's telephoto camera can reach 3x optical zoom, then crop into the massive 200MP sensor to extend that range to 6x lossless zoom. It doesn't approach the heady 10x zoom of the Find X9 Ultra, though. The Find X10 Pro Max is better equipped for macro photography, however, as it's capable of a 10cm focal distance on its 3x periscope telephoto lens.
More broadly, when pitted against the Find X9 Pro, I was pleasantly surprised to see that this year's X10 Pro Max autofocuses better in low light and captures more detail, regardless of the shooting mode I used.
The Find X10 series' default setup will process full-res 200MP images into 26MP images across its entire zoom range, which is a nice touch and means less fussing around in the settings. Naturally, you can choose a high-res shooting mode if you want every single pixel.
There are plenty of features for video power users, too. Oppo claims its new DeepPix technology, which is built into Samsung's ISOCELL HPC sensor, delivers up to 17 stops of dynamic range, helping it capture in both bright and dimly lit environments. I didn't notice substantial dynamic range improvements in stills, but the technology is aimed more at video, preserving detail in high-contrast scenes.
The Find X10 Pro seems less prone to blown-out footage in bright light, but early testing suggests incremental improvement rather than a headline feature. If you're a vlogger or dedicated smartphone videographer, you'll appreciate the slight upgrade here, although many may not even notice it.
Those video pros have plenty of other modes to play with, too. The X10 Pro Max's Pro Video mode offers open-gate capture, using each sensor's full imaging area for wider coverage and giving editors more latitude to crop and reframe footage in post-production. It also supports Oppo's O-Log2 format, LUT previewing and support for Blackmagic's camera app. If you're going all-in, Oppo also teamed up with Tilta for a KHRONOS creator kit, with a phone cage, grip, cooling fan and flash.
The teleconvertor system makes a return and feels less flimsy this time around. Composed of a specialized case, teleconvertor lens (which looks like a silencer for a pistol) and lens plate, it's a fun (optional) addition to the Find X10 Pro Max's camera offering.
The teleconvertor lens itself is the same as the Find X9 Pro's, but you will need a new adapter plate and case for the Find X10 Pro Max. With the Find X9 Pro, the telephoto lens plate that slides onto the felt a little too much like an early prototype. Over time, the black finish also scraped off after repeated removal, which had to be done often because the plate obscured the other camera sensors.
The new lens mounting plate sadly has the same issue: It covers those other 200MP sensors when you use the...

title_en: Now you can chat with Gemini while using Google Maps through CarPlay
title_fa: Now you can chat with Gemini while using Google Maps through CarPlay
excerpt_en: Just tap the new Gemini icon to get started.
excerpt_fa: Just tap the new Gemini icon to get started.
content_en:
Now you can chat with Gemini while using Google Maps through CarPlay
Just tap the new Gemini icon to get started.
If you're one of the many CarPlay users who prefers Google Maps for navigation, Google has begun rolling out a small but meaningful update for the iOS version of Maps. Now you can use the company's conversational driving experience, Gemini in navigation, through CarPlay. With Maps open, you'll see a new Gemini icon toward the bottom right of the interface. Just tap the bottom to start asking questions of the company's chatbot.
"It's a conversational way to find stops on-the-go, report traffic disruptions, get information about places, and more," Google explains, adding Gemini is particularly adept at answering multi-part questions like "what park is famous for gorgeous views overlooking the city?" Gemini in navigation is starting to roll out today to CarPlay users in the US and throughout the world. As always, it may take a few days before the update arrives on your device, so be patient if you don't see it right away.
The update arrives after Google yesterday announced it was beginning to roll out Gemini Personal Intelligence to Android Auto users. When enabled, the feature allows the chatbot to pull information from your other Google apps to personalize its responses. In practice, Google says Personal Intelligence improves Gemini's reasoning capabilities makes the assistant capable of delivering more specific details as they relate to your questions and prompts.

title_en: A permanent Pokémon store will open in London, with more locations outside Asia to follow
title_fa: A permanent Pokémon store will open in London, with more locations outside Asia to follow
excerpt_en: The new retail location is set to open by 2029.
excerpt_fa: The new retail location is set to open by 2029.
content_en:
A permanent Pokémon store will open in London, with more locations outside Asia to follow
The new retail location is set to open by 2029.
As it stands, Pokémon fans outside of Asia either have to travel to the continent or hope for a pop-up closer to home if they want to spend (probably lots of) money at one of the brand's physical retail locations. That's changing, though, as The Pokémon Company says it's opening several permanent stores outside of Asia. The first of those will be in London and it's slated to open by 2029.
Pop-up Pokémon shops have appeared in London in the past, including one at the Natural History Museum earlier this year and others during various editions of the Pokémon European International Championships. As with the pop-ups, the permanent location will have exclusive merch.
"We are always exploring new opportunities that help us create unique and memorable experiences for our fans," Gaku Susai, The Pokémon Company International's chief product and experience officer said. "This new London store will give visitors the chance to step into the world of Pokémon, whether they're discovering the brand for the first time or have been Trainers for years."
The Pokémon Company said it will reveal details about other physical locations in the future. If it ends up bringing a store to New York, that wouldn't be its first one in the city. Pokémon Center New York opened in 2001. Four years later, that location was turned into Nintendo's flagship physical store.

title_en: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
title_fa: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
excerpt_en: Foursquare raised $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, but its equity holders saw no returns from its final acquisition.
excerpt_fa: Foursquare raised $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, but its equity holders saw no returns from its final acquisition.
content_en:
Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post, Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale.
Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor, inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome.
“I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare — the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth … nothing?” he said in the post.
Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and in 2021 brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value.
Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024.
Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps. After Foursquare, startups like Zenly and Jagat, along with Instagram and Snapchat, have explored social maps.

title_en: Stranger Than Heaven builds its identity as Like A Dragon's more relentless spin-off
title_fa: Stranger Than Heaven builds its identity as Like A Dragon's more relentless spin-off
excerpt_en: We played several hours of Sega's next big crime-thriller, and so far the Like a Dragon series is getting its most bold entry to date.
excerpt_fa: We played several hours of Sega's next big crime-thriller, and so far the Like a Dragon series is getting its most bold entry to date.
content_en:
Stranger Than Heaven builds its identity as Like A Dragon's more relentless spin-off
We played several hours of Sega's next big crime-thriller, and so far the Like a Dragon series is getting its most bold entry to date.
Stranger Than Heaven is the next game in Sega's sprawling crime-epic series Like A Dragon (formerly known as Yakuza in the US). On the surface, it looks like a grittier, more brutal take on the traditional Like a Dragon brawler action, but after extended hands-on time, I found myself thinking that Stranger Than Heaven's style feels much more grounded, and personal.
I recently spent several hours playing the opening chapters of developer RGG Studio's next entry in the crime saga, and it was clear that Stranger Than Heaven is about returning the series to its roots with a more relentless, character-driven story about an outsider making his way in early 1900s Japan. It took me a while to get into the Stranger Than Heaven's grittier crime-thriller flow, which leans heavily on a new, unusual combat system. Still, I couldn't help but be captivated by protagonist Makoto Daito's story of a stranger trying to embrace his ancestral land that's going through great change.
Japan, circa 1915, 1929, 1943, 1951, and 1965
Spanning five decades, Stranger Than Heaven follows Makoto Daito's rise from a mysterious Japanese-American outcast to an infamous hustler and gangster in 1900s Japan. Starting from his traumatic life in the segregated United States, to his eventual arrival in Japan, Daito's growth leads him to being a scrappy dock and factory worker hustling on the streets of Kokura, to an up-and-coming nightclub owner and businessman in Osaka, and eventually to one of the key figures of the Tojo Clan in 1960s Shinjuku, shaping the lives of Kazuma Kiryu and Ichiban Kasuga in future entries.
Stranger Than Heaven is a standalone story, but it also offers some intriguing narrative flooring for the Like a Dragon series. The series also balances over-the-top action and goofy humor with its enduring protagonists, and its spin-offs tackle even more off-the-wall experiences, like turn-based RPG combat and arcade-style action, while keeping the serious tone.

After fleeing from corrupt police officers in San Francisco in 1915, who accuse him of a crime he did not commit due to his race, Daito travels to Japan and discovers a different kind of racial prejudice and bigotry that he has to endure. This is an immediately effective perspective for a protagonist, especially in a Like a Dragon game.
It's structurally similar to previous games, where you explore semi-open-world towns with activities and fights outside the main story objective — all with the intent to draw you into not just the setting, but the different eras of time. With the added context of having to endure racial slurs and other forms of bigotry from townsfolk when exploring the town, and outright brutality from citizens who want to fight, it adds a new layer of immersion for Daito's story that's more grounded and unnerving than the likes of Kazuma and Ichiban.

Still, I felt that RGG Studio's handling of the tense, uncomfortable aspects of open racism is often well-intentioned and mostly well handled, presenting both the outward hostility and passive-aggressiveness of bigotry in a way that feels educational for the time period.

Stranger Than Heaven really leans into the classic Like a Dragon action-brawler experience. Still, its most evident gameplay twist is its more dynamic, complex combat system. Instead of a beat-em-up approach, the combat favors a more measured, intricate system that gives players precise control over Daito's individual arms in action. On the controller, the left shoulder buttons control Daito's light and heavy left-handed strikes, and the right shoulder button controls his light and heavy right-handed strikes. title_en: How to spot a white label gadget, and why that's important
title_fa: How to spot a white label gadget, and why that's important
excerpt_en: Sometimes the same product is sold under multiple brands, which means you might not be getting the best gear.
excerpt_fa: Sometimes the same product is sold under multiple brands, which means you might not be getting the best gear.
content_en:
How to spot a white label gadget, and why that's important
Forewarned is forearmed, after all.
A few weeks ago, the Engadget team was swapping war stories about covering tech in the face of an ever-growing glut of white label devices. Tech, pumped out by a single factory, then sold on to others who put their name on it to sell. They're often attached to a Zombie Brand, as it's an easy way to sell mediocre tech to an unsuspecting public. That's not to say white label tech is bad per se, but it helps to know what you're buying before you hand your money over. So I've sketched out this brief spotter's guide to make sure you're not going to get duped.
White labels 101
Device manufacturing is the province of a small cluster of Asian factories. Very few companies actually make their own hardware. Even those with a long history of designing and building products outsource the actual work this way. White label manufacturing is a legitimate practice, and even big names will add their brand to gear made by their ostensible rivals. Take Sony, which put its name on Samsung and LG-made panels years before it sold its TV business to TCL.
But there are also plenty of generic, sometimes copycat devices, stamped out by an Original Device Manufacturer (ODM). In one example, Engadget's camera guru Steve Dent found the exact same gimbal camera available under three different names. Ordro's UHD-M5, AgfaPhoto Realimove MC3X and Minolta Showtime MN5KG100 even have identical pictures on their Amazon listings. And it's not just camera gear that is rife with products like this.
I was examining the broader smart ring market and found a whole heap of branded rings which could be traced back to a single ODM, J-Style. On its website, J-Style says it offers a rapid white label service for its rings, including custom packaging and logo placement. And it appears the rings offered by Fittr, Qalo and Insix all use the same J-Style X1 under different names. On a similar note, the Reebok/F50 smart ring, which is sold by The Original Fit Factory, looks awfully similar to J-Style's X6 ring.
How to spot a white label
You already know the easiest and smartest thing to do before buying any product is look it up on the internet. I'd advise skipping the AI overview in favor of actual reviews both from sites like this one, and on social media platforms like Reddit. If something's not very good, or comes from a brand with a less than stellar reputation, it's going to be hard to keep that fact quiet for long. If there are no reviews beyond customer recommendations on the product page, it's a sign the company is looking to avoid the scrutiny that comes from being independently reviewed.
Brand
The biggest names in the technology industry have taken a lot of time and effort to build trust with the public. If the name is particularly weighty, the less likely they are to risk it with a low-effort product produced by an unnamed third party. Oftentimes, it's the medium-sized company that's happier to license the brand to third parties for products outside their usual domain.
A good example here is Reebok, a company known for making footwear and apparel and apparel-related things. But you can also buy Reebok-branded exercise equipment (RFE International), Reebok-branded eyewear (Mondottica), a Reebok-branded smart ring (The Original Fit Factory), Reebok-branded smart glasses (by Lucyd) and a Reebok-branded smartwatch (CE Brands/Vitalist).
Similarly, a formerly notable tech giant like Motorola, which is now Lenovo's mobile brand, is happy to license its name. The company ceased making its own wearables nearly a decade ago, and its watches since then were made by licensees. This can wind up backfiring and hurting the brand if the product sold under the name isn't very good. I can only speak to my time with the 2026 Moto Watch (also by CE Brands/Vitalist).
At the bottom of the pile are the Zombie Brands, names from a few years back which have been picked up for pennies at a bankruptcy auction. These are snapped up by various ODMs or their partners for a memorable name to slap on an otherwise cheap product. One of the most notable must be Kodak, which has had its brand sliced and shared out among so many companies it's hard to keep track.
Track record and the pitch
A crucial benefit of the white label process, for both new companies and zombie brands, is that it's an easy way to enter a new market. If you're a company looking to enter the gadget space, harnessing an ODM is a quick and easy way to do so without a lot of risk. At least, not to them, since most of the risk is taken on by the consumer parting with cash for the product.
That's a useful tell for wary customers, since if your local bakery suddenly starts selling smart glasses, you can probably guess they didn't make it. If a company enters a space it's had no experience in, and they don't spend a lot of time talking about the product, it's a white label. Sure, it's not unheard of that an analog company would enter the tech space, but they'll also be more than willing to spend hours talking about it.
In fact, that's true for most tech companies, since they sure love to talk about the process which led to the product's creation. Even for the most mundane devices, they'll wheel a designer out to wax lyrical about the improvements they've made to the product.
Amazon
If you're worried the gadget you're looking to buy could be from a white label, it's often good to look on Amazon. As part of the whole "low cost, low effort" nature of these devices, you'll often find the same device sold under multiple names by multiple brands. Often, they'll be marketed using the same set of images supplied by the ODM, resulting in a scroll of products which all look the same. Or it's the same initial render with the odd tweak, because one company has their own pricey Photoshop subscription.
For instance, let's take a look at the low-end fitness tracker market where Xiaomi's various bands reign supreme....

title_en: Here's how SpaceX plans to catch Starship's upper stage for the first time
title_fa: Here's how SpaceX plans to catch Starship's upper stage for the first time
excerpt_en: SpaceX has released a demo showing how it intends to catch Starship's upper stage, which could happen as soon as next month.
excerpt_fa: SpaceX has released a demo showing how it intends to catch Starship's upper stage, which could happen as soon as next month.
content_en:
Here's how SpaceX plans to catch Starship's upper stage for the first time
Elon Musk says SpaceX will attempt to capture both the vehicle’s lower and upper stages for test flight 15.
SpaceX is planning to catch both the Starship's Super Heavy booster and its upper stage, dubbed the "Ship," for the first time ever for the vehicle's 15th flight test. During the company's earnings call, which was livestreamed on X, Elon Musk announced SpaceX's plan for the flight that could take place as soon as next month. SpaceX also showed a short video during the livestream, demonstrating how it intends to safely retrieve the Ship when it makes its way back to Earth.
You can watch the SpaceX earnings call and fast forward to 1:07:19 to watch the simulation, but you can also watch the excerpt below, courtesy of investor Sawyer Merritt.
As you can see, the company intends to catch the Ship using the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower, which it had also used in the past to capture the vehicle's Super Heavy booster. While both of the vehicle's stages splashed into the ocean for test flight 14, SpaceX's ultimate goal is to develop Starship into a fully and rapidly reusable orbital launch vehicle for future deep space missions. It was, after all, designed with the purpose of carrying crew and cargo to the moon and to Mars in mind. If the company manages to catch both stages next month, it would be a huge step towards achieving that goal.
As Space notes, the company has yet to try capturing Starship's upper stage, as it travels higher and farther than the booster. It's faster as well. For Flight 14, for instance, Ship was supposed to spend 10 hours in orbit, circling our planet. SpaceX ultimately had to cut the trip short, because one of Ship's engines malfunctioned, but it still took hours to return to Earth, whereas Super Heavy came back just a few minutes after launch.

title_en: Apple iPhone Duo review: A first-class foldable
title_fa: Apple iPhone Duo review: A first-class foldable
excerpt_en: Even though it's heavy and expensive, Apple's first foldable handset is a treat for iPhone users unwilling to switch to Android.
excerpt_fa: Even though it's heavy and expensive, Apple's first foldable handset is a treat for iPhone users unwilling to switch to Android.
content_en:
Apple iPhone Duo review: A first-class foldable
But a lot of apps still need fine-tuning to look their best on Apple’s first bendy iPhone.
Nearly a decade ago, the iPhone X ushered in major changes to the way Apple built its mobile devices and we are still seeing the effects of that today. However, between John Ternus taking the reins as CEO and the arrival of the iPhone Duo ($1,999), it feels like Apple has embarked upon another paradigm shift that could pave the way for the company's next generation of hardware. While the Duo is heavy, expensive and late to the market compared to its Android rivals, it encompasses some of the best tech used by its competitors while also redeeming features that other manufacturers have seemingly left for dead. And even though many apps still need to be optimized to fully take advantage of the Duo's design, the release of Apple's first foldable has been worth the wait.
Design and displays
The move from one to two screens offers a world of possibilities for phone makers, but also a lot of traps. You make something too sleek and it might not have the durability to withstand the rigors of everyday life. And with not one but two displays to worry about, the handoff between from one panel to another becomes even more important. To balance things out, Apple went with a design that delivers strength and consistency, even though the downside of that decision is a device that's significantly heavier than its closest competitors.
On the outside, the Duo features a glossy 1,878 x 2,670 5.4-inch OLED display with 120Hz ProMotion support and an impressive peak brightness of up to 3,000 nits. Meanwhile on the inside, there's a larger 1,398 x 2,034 7.6-inch panel with a matching 1:1.4 aspect ratio and lofty luminance. This makes transitioning from one screen to another super smooth, as you get the same viewing experience (homescreen and all), just with twice as much real estate to work with. Additionally, Apple's clever opening animation adds a bit of visual spice to tie everything together.
The one major difference is that the Duo's inside screen has a matte nanotexture finish instead of a glossy treatment which serves a few purposes. Not only does it help protect the rest of the flexible display underneath, it also cuts down on reflections while hiding the appearance of a crease. To be clear, there is definitely a small divot that runs down the middle of the main display and if you're looking for it at the right angle, it's not hard to find. That said, during normal use when you're looking at the phone head on, the crease basically disappears. A word of caution: While it is replaceable (for a $49 fee), the Duo's nanotexture layer can be removed if you pick at it too much. And unlike with its Android rivals, there's no warning during setup that this film should not be peeled off by anyone aside from Apple-certified technicians.
Regardless, the iPhone Duo's two displays both provide excellent image quality. Its exterior display is a great size for one-handed use and the textured surface on its main panel should make drawing or taking notes with an Apple Pencil feel great (support for that arrives later this month). I also think the strong matte finish makes things like comics and anime look even better than they typically do on glossy screens. The small trade-off is that perceived color saturation and vividness from the Duo's interior panel isn't quite as pronounced in bright rooms, though at night, that deficiency goes away.
Elsewhere, the Duo is held together by a burly titanium chassis and one of the nicest hinges I've used on any foldable. Apple says it's composed of more than 100 different components, but you'd never know just from using it because it's so damn smooth. It can hold itself open in a huge range of positions while the amount of pressure needed to unfold the device changes the wider you go, which adds an extra level of sophistication when switching between screens. And somehow amongst all this, Apple found a way to give the Duo an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, which is only available from one other family of foldables on sale in the US: the Pixel 11 Pro Fold line.
Notably, instead of Face ID, which has become a standard feature on modern iPhones, the Duo uses a Touch ID sensor built into the lock button on the side. This might seem like a weird choice, but on a device that's meant to be used in a ton of positions, the idea of having to put infrared face readers on both the inside and outside of the phone just doesn't make a ton of sense. Thankfully, Apple's solution is really accurate, though it does take a bit longer to unlock than you might expect. The company says the thought process behind this is that this creates a more consistent experience when compared to other devices that still use Touch ID (like iPads and MacBooks). Apple says this also gives the phone a chance to wake up and display things like notifications on your lock screen before you get access to the entire device.
The main drawback to the Duo's beefy build is that it weighs 254 grams (8.96 ounces), which is more than 25 percent heavier than a Galaxy Z Fold 8, despite the latter having the same number of cameras and larger displays. And that's before you factor in the extra heft from a case. This kind of bulk is pretty significant to the point where the Duo can feel a bit like an anchor in your pocket if you're wearing loose pants and during longer sessions, so you'll probably want to hold the Duo with two hands instead of one.
Performance and software
Powered by an A20 Pro chip, the same as what you get in an iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo has no shortage of processing power. That said, I won't belabor you with too many anecdotes of how fast Apple's first foldable is. The Duo pumps out strong framerates while gaming and running multiple apps side-by-side is a breeze. You can technically even play multiple games at the same time thanks to the Duo's multitasking capabilities,...

And with not one but two displays to worry about, the handoff between from one panel to another becomes even more important. To balance things out, Apple went with a design that delivers strength and consistency, even though the downside of that decision is a device that's significantly heavier than its closest competitors.
On the outside, the Duo features a glossy 1,878 x 2,670 5.4-inch OLED display with 120Hz ProMotion support and an impressive peak brightness of up to 3,000 nits. Meanwhile on the inside, there's a larger 1,398 x 2,034 7.6-inch panel with a matching 1:1.4 aspect ratio and lofty luminance. This makes transitioning from one screen to another super smooth, as you get the same viewing experience (homescreen and all), just with twice as much real estate to work with. Additionally, Apple's clever opening animation adds a bit of visual spice to tie everything together.
The one major difference is that the Duo's inside screen has a matte nanotexture finish instead of a glossy treatment which serves a few purposes. Not only does it help protect the rest of the flexible display underneath, it also cuts down on reflections while hiding the appearance of a crease. To be clear, there is definitely a small divot that runs down the middle of the main display and if you're looking for it at the right angle, it's not hard to find. That said, during normal use when you're looking at the phone head on, the crease basically disappears. A word of caution: While it is replaceable (for a $49 fee), the Duo's nanotexture layer can be removed if you pick at it too much. And unlike with its Android rivals, there's no warning during setup that this film should not be peeled off by anyone aside from Apple-certified technicians.
Regardless, the iPhone Duo's two displays both provide excellent image quality. Its exterior display is a great size for one-handed use and the textured surface on its main panel should make drawing or taking notes with an Apple Pencil feel great (support for that arrives later this month). I also think the strong matte finish makes things like comics and anime look even better than they typically do on glossy screens. The small trade-off is that perceived color saturation and vividness from the Duo's interior panel isn't quite as pronounced in bright rooms, though at night, that deficiency goes away.
Elsewhere, the Duo is held together by a burly titanium chassis and one of the nicest hinges I've used on any foldable. Apple says it's composed of more than 100 different components, but you'd never know just from using it because it's so damn smooth. It can hold itself open in a huge range of positions while the amount of pressure needed to unfold the device changes the wider you go, which adds an extra level of sophistication when switching between screens. And somehow amongst all this, Apple found a way to give the Duo an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, which is only available from one other family of foldables on sale in the US: the Pixel 11 Pro Fold line.
Notably, instead of Face ID, which has become a standard feature on modern iPhones, the Duo uses a Touch ID sensor built into the lock button on the side. This might seem like a weird choice, but on a device that's meant to be used in a ton of positions, the idea of having to put infrared face readers on both the inside and outside of the phone just doesn't make a ton of sense. Thankfully, Apple's solution is really accurate, though it does take a bit longer to unlock than you might expect. The company says the thought process behind this is that this creates a more consistent experience when compared to other devices that still use Touch ID (like iPads and MacBooks). Apple says this also gives the phone a chance to wake up and display things like notifications on your lock screen before you get access to the entire device.
The main drawback to the Duo's beefy build is that it weighs 254 grams (8.96 ounces), which is more than 25 percent heavier than a Galaxy Z Fold 8, despite the latter having the same number of cameras and larger displays. And that's before you factor in the extra heft from a case. This kind of bulk is pretty significant to the point where the Duo can feel a bit like an anchor in your pocket if you're wearing loose pants and during longer sessions, so you'll probably want to hold the Duo with two hands instead of one.
Performance and software
Powered by an A20 Pro chip, the same as what you get in an iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo has no shortage of processing power. That said, I won't belabor you with too many anecdotes of how fast Apple's first foldable is. The Duo pumps out strong framerates while gaming and running multiple apps side-by-side is a breeze. You can technically even play multiple games at the same time thanks to the Duo's multitasking capabilities,...

title_en: Two dangerous internet security issues are putting site admins on edge
title_fa: Two dangerous internet security issues are putting site admins on edge
excerpt_en: The web is a bit of a hot mess today following the discovery of two severe vulnerabilities.
excerpt_fa: The web is a bit of a hot mess today following the discovery of two severe vulnerabilities.
content_en:
Two dangerous internet security issues are putting site admins on edge
Both problems could result in large-scale attacks and require massive cleanup.
The web is a bit of a hot mess today following the discovery of two severe vulnerabilities, according to security releases seen by Ars Technica. The first involves TLS certificates with extremely weak encryption that could affect everything from VPNs to IoT devices. The other is a severe PHP programming language vulnerability impacting CMS systems including WordPress and Drupal. Both problems could result in large-scale attacks and require massive cleanup jobs, security experts said.
gPHP Foundation said on X that it's releasing security patches for two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2 out of 10 on the severity scale. Ahead of the release today at 14:00 UTC (10AM ET), the group said that "PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update," adding that it will issue an "earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence."
The advisory follows a report showing video of a tool called PHP2Shell running code on web servers including the latest versions of WordPress, MediaWiki, Symphony, Drupal and other PHP-based sites. The security firm watchTowr claims it has confirmed the vulnerability and that it affects every version from PHP 5 (2004) onward. "According to an unverified report, the vulnerability would let an attacker run their own code on a server running PHP, potentially taking control of it," watchTowr's FAQ on the exploit states.
Another company, Sansec, said it expects "mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release." With all this, web admins are likely scrambling to patch the issue, so some PHP-based websites could go down briefly while that happens.
The other issue with TLS certificates is a whole other bag of excrement. An India-based firm called eMudhra said eight of its intermediate CA certificates have been compromised that "chain to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores." The issue is that the private keys are weak and could let attackers forge credentials for a range of websites and apps.
The compromised private key sizes ranged from three to eight bits, rather than the usual 384 bits. Specifically, the private keys used by eMudhra were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237, according to Hacker News and other reports. Those would allow anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers.
The eMudhra certificates were widely trusted by hosts like Cloudflare, as well as browsers, operating systems, IoT (Internet of Things) and other devices that connect to the internet. Once they forge domain certificates, attackers can use those domains to impersonate servers and intercept traffic.
Mozilla, Google and Apple have blocked the compromised certificates for their browsers. However, Mozilla's security expert Dennis Jackson warned that a macOS utility may keep trusting the compromised certificates as it doesn't check for revocation information — something that applies to many other clients as well. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates and blamed a script used to generate them.
As it stands, the biggest risk is currently to VPNs, particularly where governments actively try to intercept traffic. However, it may also impact IoT devices, unmaintained servers and other parts of the net. "This will be a massive cleanup job, bigger than Heartbleed," cryptography engineer Filippo Valsorda told Ars, referring to a previous TLS bug that caused mass attacks back in 2014.

title_en: OpenAI's agents disabled their own safety monitoring systems
title_fa: OpenAI's agents disabled their own safety monitoring systems
excerpt_en: OpenAI reveals that its agents misbehaved by switching off the system monitoring them for misbehaviors.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI reveals that its agents misbehaved by switching off the system monitoring them for misbehaviors.
content_en:
OpenAI's agents disabled their own safety monitoring systems
The company says it’s assessing whether its agents have the ‘propensity to evade misalignment monitoring.’
OpenAI's agents misbehaved by switching off the systems meant to monitor them for misbehavior, or in AI parlance, misalignment. In the latest post on the company's Alignment Research Blog, it reported two instances of agents weakening its misalignment monitoring systems while they were working on software changes.
In the first incident, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team. It happened on October 3, when a staff member asked the agent to create evaluation tasks using employee feedback collected via Slack. They told the agent, as part of the instruction, not to send any messages about the task. The agent used that instruction as the reason to stop sending the security team monitoring notifications. In another incident that took place on October 6, a GPT-6 Astra agent that was migrating a program removed OpenAI's monitoring system and then falsely told the user that it didn't disable it.
Last month, OpenAI canceled the launch of GPT-6.1 Astra, because it reportedly showed higher levels of deception than its predecessors during internal testing. The models involved in these cases are already available to the public, but they still displayed deceptive behaviors. Just imagine how much more deceitful GPT-6.1 Astra is for the company to pull its planned launch this month.
Both incidents happened during internal coding tasks and didn't result in a third-party website or service getting hacked. But OpenAI says it's making it harder for agents to disable monitoring, and it's also evaluating whether the cases mean its agents have the "propensity to evade misalignment monitoring." AI companies have promised to be better at preventing and reporting misalignment incidents involving their models and agents, after reports came out one after the other that they broke free from their isolated testing environments and infiltrated third-party services.
In OpenAI's case, it admitted back in July that the agents it was testing broke into AI repository Hugging Face. It even revealed later on that its agents created a message board to share exploits with each other. The company self-reported other incidents, as well, including ones wherein its agents hacked into or meddled with US government websites.

title_en: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
title_fa: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
excerpt_en: YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike...
excerpt_fa: YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike...
content_en:
YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them.
YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
Some users have reported that their YouTube dislike button has been moved to the three-dots menu.
Some users have reported that their YouTube dislike button has been moved to the three-dots menu.
Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. Moving it to a submenu would make it considerably more of an effort to access, meaning that fewer people would likely use it.
It’s unclear how widely this apparent test may be rolled out, and Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
YouTube has shown a willingness to make changes to the dislike button. In 2021, it hid the public dislike count on videos to help “protect creators from harassment,” though creators can still see dislike counts. Earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button from YouTube Shorts, suggesting instead that users take advantage of options in the three-dots menu.

title_en: How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
title_fa: How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
excerpt_en: A 1 kW wind turbine can help with your electric bill, but the wind determines how much.
excerpt_fa: A 1 kW wind turbine can help with your electric bill, but the wind determines how much.
content_en:
How much power can a 1kW wind turbine produce for your home?
It all depends on the wind.
Do home wind turbines actually work? The answer is a very reserved "yes." With solar energy cruising into record territory, small-scale wind power for residential use tends to get lost in the sun (poor pun intended).There are several caveats, though wind power is not an altogether losing proposition. It really depends on the need and the scale of use. They even make compact turbines for powering RVs, so it also depends on your definition of "home."
It's important to note that a 1 kW turbine is a "peak" power measure, not necessarily what you'll get out of it. The more useful number to look at is annual or monthly energy production, measured in kilowatt-hours. In a carefully chosen position, a 1 kW turbine could feasibly produce 200 kWh per month, or about 2,400 kWh per year. That works out to under a quarter of the average US household's annual energy consumption.
None of this is to say that wind turbines are weak power producers — it just depends on the wind. If you live in an area with annual wind speeds averaging 14+ mph, this is something worth looking into. If not, or if windy days are sparse or even average, maybe not so much. A 1 kW system is feasible, but it's best to look at it in terms of supplemental power for an already efficient home.
Placement determines whether it works
A wind turbine for a home practically requires a high average wind speed that's consistent month-to-month. Homes with lots of trees, surrounded by other homes, behind hills or with large sheds need not apply. Not only do these obstacles block wind, but they also create turbulence, which reduces output and speeds up wear and tear on the turbine. The Department of Energy's small wind guidance recommends placing the bottom of the rotor at least 30 feet above any obstacle within 300 horizontal feet of the tower.
That recommendation alone tells you all you need to know about placing a wind turbine in a suburban neighborhood. It'll make for some interesting conversations at the neighbor's house, and little more. Worse, most local zoning rules limit structures to around 35 feet, and wind turbines often require much more in order to clear nearby trees and rooftops. A rooftop installation option sounds great on paper, but it can transmit vibration and noise directly into your rooftop, a lovely side effect while trying to catch some Zs before work.
If you're sold on wind power, look beyond your region's wind map, check local zoning and utility rules and conduct a thorough assessment of your site's obstacles and average wind direction. It's also a good idea to get an installer to estimate overall production before spending your hard-earned dough.
A whole-house turbine needs much more capacity
If your home is a small, economical little cabin or a permanently parked RV, a 1kW wind turbine is certainly an option. However, it's not enough to power a typical US home. The average household uses about 10,500 kWh of electricity per year (around 850 kWh per month), and a residential turbine in the 5 kW to 15 kW range is necessary to put a dent in that power consumption.
Cost is another reason to proceed with a bit of caution. It'll run the average consumer between $20,000 and $50,000 to toss up a wind turbine. Installing solar panels with the same energy production in mind is roughly $2,500 to $3,500, and that's before incentives are calculated in.
A grid-connected system typically requires an inverter as well and can offset some utility use when the wind is blowing. Off-grid systems will require batteries and a charge controller to store power. For the majority of suburban dwellers, improving insulation and tossing in some ground- or roof-mounted solar panels will provide more dependable, solid results. If you want to go the wind route, it makes the most sense in open, rural areas that have verified average wind speeds and a place to put your tower.

title_en: What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
title_fa: What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
excerpt_en: Here's what your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button can really do, from launching workouts and retracing routes to controlling smart home devices with one tap.
excerpt_fa: Here's what your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button can really do, from launching workouts and retracing routes to controlling smart home devices with one tap.
content_en:
What can you use your Apple Watch Ultra 4 action button for?
That little orange button can do a lot more than start your next workout.
If you're serious about running, hiking, weightlifting or other high-energy activities, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is easy to recommend. At $800, it is a commitment — but that's surprisingly reasonable compared to other fitness and adventure watches, and the benefits over a regular Apple Watch aren't trivial. It's bigger, tougher and lasts up to 50 hours on a charge, whereas a Series 12 has to be topped up every day. Combined with its satellite features and GPS accuracy, it might legitimately save your life on a wilderness trek.
An Ultra difference that Apple tends to downplay these days is the action button. It's an orange button next to the speaker grille, used as a quick shortcut for commands that other Watch owners have to tap through menus or complications to reach. It can also activate the watch's emergency siren, which helps attract attention if you're lost or injured. It's such an obvious, low-cost feature that it's almost insulting that it's not on Series devices, too.
There's a broad range of commands you can assign to the button. You can only assign one at a time, but if you know what you're doing, it can be immensely useful for anything that's a daily habit. All the more so if you take advantage of the automation upgrades in watchOS 27 and iOS 27.
The action button arsenal on your wrist
If you hold down the action button briefly, you'll see the Quick Switch menu appear. This lets you swap the button's single-tap function on the fly, which can be vital for some activities, particularly outdoor navigation. You'll see what we mean in a moment.
The most straightforward options are Flashlight, Voice Memo, Translate and Recognize Music. With these, you just hit the button once to start the function and again to stop it. As a side note, Recognize Music should be nearly instant on an Ultra 4, thanks to Apple's new Audio Intelligence capabilities, which also support automatic Shazam detection.
Slightly more complex are Workout, Stopwatch and Dive. With Stopwatch, pressing the button once starts timing, and pressing it again marks a lap. Press the action and side buttons simultaneously to pause. With Dive, a regular press begins your aquatic adventures, while pressing action and side simultaneously launches an app-specific secondary function.
Similarly, Workout will either open the Workout app or immediately launch into a particular activity. You can change this by going to Settings > Action Button. Mid-session, tapping the button performs a secondary function, such as marking a segment. To pause, press action and side together.
Special attention is due to the two navigation options, Waypoint and Backtrack. The first drops waypoints visible in the Compass app and the Waypoint watchface, although some waypoints are added automatically, such as your parked car and the last available cell signal. Backtrack is also linked to the Compass app, but tapping once starts recording a precise route you can retrace later. Hitting the action and side buttons simultaneously flips between the Record and Retrace modes.
The showstoppers: Accessibility and Shortcuts
For some users, assigning the button to Accessibility might be unavoidable. This lets you trigger things like AssistiveTouch, VoiceOver and even control nearby devices. There may be a reason to use this if you're fully able-bodied, too, so check it out.
Arguably, though, the single most powerful action is Shortcut. This is configured like Accessibility, but lets you trigger any automation you've built in the iPhone's Shortcuts app. Given that these automations can stretch across multiple platforms and even control smart home accessories, there's virtually unlimited potential. A single tap might, for example, turn on your lights, adjust your thermostat and even start playing local news on your HomePod.
The Shortcuts app can be unwieldy at times. Thankfully, a big change in iOS 27 on iPhones with Apple Intelligence is the ability to build shortcuts simply by describing what you want them to do. This greatly simplifies the process, although it's important to double-check the results. You don't want an "I'm driving home" routine to accidentally send an ETA to your mother-in-law instead of your partner.

Press the action and side buttons simultaneously to pause. With Dive, a regular press begins your aquatic adventures, while pressing action and side simultaneously launches an app-specific secondary function.
Similarly, Workout will either open the Workout app or immediately launch into a particular activity. You can change this by going to Settings > Action Button. Mid-session, tapping the button performs a secondary function, such as marking a segment. To pause, press action and side together.
Special attention is due to the two navigation options, Waypoint and Backtrack. The first drops waypoints visible in the Compass app and the Waypoint watchface, although some waypoints are added automatically, such as your parked car and the last available cell signal. Backtrack is also linked to the Compass app, but tapping once starts recording a precise route you can retrace later. Hitting the action and side buttons simultaneously flips between the Record and Retrace modes.
The showstoppers: Accessibility and Shortcuts
For some users, assigning the button to Accessibility might be unavoidable. This lets you trigger things like AssistiveTouch, VoiceOver and even control nearby devices. There may be a reason to use this if you're fully able-bodied, too, so check it out.
Arguably, though, the single most powerful action is Shortcut. This is configured like Accessibility, but lets you trigger any automation you've built in the iPhone's Shortcuts app. Given that these automations can stretch across multiple platforms and even control smart home accessories, there's virtually unlimited potential. A single tap might, for example, turn on your lights, adjust your thermostat and even start playing local news on your HomePod.
The Shortcuts app can be unwieldy at times. Thankfully, a big change in iOS 27 on iPhones with Apple Intelligence is the ability to build shortcuts simply by describing what you want them to do. This greatly simplifies the process, although it's important to double-check the results. You don't want an "I'm driving home" routine to accidentally send an ETA to your mother-in-law instead of your partner.

content_en:
On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed.
Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
Ann Altman’s lawsuit against her brother was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled.
Ann Altman’s lawsuit against her brother was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled.
When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, “Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.”
Bluestone granted Sam Altman’s motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled in that court, while denying Sam’s request for attorney fees and costs. Santos Perez, a lawyer who had represented Ann until withdrawing this month, told The Guardian in a statement that “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

title_en: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
title_fa: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
excerpt_en: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
excerpt_fa: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
content_en:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.
Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.
Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.
The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”
Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.
It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.
The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.
Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.
Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

title_en: Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
title_fa: Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
excerpt_en: Oura has updated its smart rings with new cardio fitness-related metrics, including VO2 Max estimates.
excerpt_fa: Oura has updated its smart rings with new cardio fitness-related metrics, including VO2 Max estimates.
content_en:
Oura Ring can track new stats related to cardio fitness
The smart rings are getting Cardio Effort and VO2 Max data.
Smart ring company Oura announced that it is adding two new fitness features. First is Cardio Effort, an assessment of how much strain the wearer has put on their body during activity. The personalized metric will offer five ranges — light, fair, maintaining, building and reaching — that offer a gauge of how the week's activities compare to the individual's baseline. The feature is based on the Training Impulse method and is designed to monitor long-term trends in cardiovascular activity, the company said.
The second feature is that the smart rings will automatically estimate VO2 Max stats. This feature was previously called Cardio Capacity in the Oura Labs tool. It wasn't an automatic metric and it required a six-minute walking test before it could be enabled. The revised VO2 Max makes passive estimations on regular GPS-enabled workouts, meaning the test is no longer needed. VO2 Max stats will be available in Oura Labs for the third-generation Oura Ring and later models.
These new additions further expand Oura's offerings for holistic health data. Other wearables, including the Apple Watch and Fitbit, have been able to track similar cardio metrics for some time, so the change could make Oura a viable option for people who prefer the ring form factor to the watch or bracelet ones.

title_en: Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
title_fa: Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
excerpt_en: From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
excerpt_fa: From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
content_en:
Five things you should know before buying the iPhone Duo
From software limitations to the pre-sale deals, here's what you need to know ahead of the iPhone Duo launch.
Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin this Friday, and the first units will be shipped to buyers on October 23. And there's a lot of hype around the Duo, since it's the first foldable iPhone ever — and represents the most radical change to the iPhone in a while. It's also the most expensive iPhone yet, starting at $1,999. Despite the price, the device comes with some trade-offs that we've already covered in detail. It lacks some popular features and the cameras aren't the best on an iPhone. Even so, many people are eager to buy one.
But before you go ahead with your pre-order on Friday, it's worth going over all these limitations and deciding whether the iPhone Duo is really for you. Plus, there are some deals worth checking out, a few accessories to consider and reviews of competing products that you should definitely read before buying an iPhone Duo.
What you give up compared to a regular iPhone
Yes, the iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone in the lineup today — but that doesn't mean it has the best hardware in every respect. As we've previously covered, one of its biggest drawbacks is its cameras. Like midrange iPhones, the Duo has two rear cameras and no dedicated telephoto lens. You can still get a 2x "optical-quality" zoom thanks to a digital crop of the main 48-megapixel sensor, but it's nowhere near the quality of the zoom lens found on the iPhone 18 Pro. The front-facing camera also has a lower resolution compared to the latest iPhones, with only 12 megapixels instead of 18 megapixels. There's no variable aperture on the main lens either — that feature remains exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro models.
Unlocking the iPhone Duo is also different, because it relies on Touch ID on the side button instead of Face ID. It's not exactly a problem, but it might take some time to get used to. The Action Button is gone, too, so you'll be limited to silencing your phone or accessing quick controls through the Control Center. Camera Control is still there, though, so you can still quickly open your favorite camera app with just a click.
Then there's the issue of apps. Apple has optimized iOS 27 to take advantage of the new foldable form factor, and apps can do the same. This means that menus and apps can automatically snap to fit two halves of the screen when you bend the hinge, for instance. However, when it comes to third-party apps, developers will have to update them so they, too, fill the entire screen of the iPhone Duo. Some popular apps, such as Netflix, Zoom and Slack, will already have updates available for the iPhone Duo on launch day, but most developers still have work to do. Expect some of your apps to look a little odd on the iPhone Duo for a while — some may appear stretched, while others may have black bars.
How the iPhone Duo compares to other foldables
It's hard not to compare the iPhone Duo to other foldable phones on the market, especially since there are so many of them out there. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is likely one of the main competitors, since they're both quite similar in terms of design. However, the Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899 — $100 less than the Duo — and is notably lighter and thinner. It weighs 201 grams (7.09 ounces) and measures 9.7mm (0.38 inches) when closed, compared to the iPhone Duo's 254 grams (8.9 ounces) and 11.3mm (0.44 inches).
Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold also starts at $1,899 and includes a telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom, which, according to our review, makes it one of the best camera systems on a foldable phone.
These comparisons are academic, of course. When it comes to getting one for yourself, you should think about the ecosystem. If you're already locked into the Apple ecosystem, the iPhone Duo is a strong choice. But if you're open to trying something different, it's definitely worth checking out the competition, too. Our comparisons of the Duo versus the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Duo versus the Pixel 11 Pro Fold go further into the details.
The deals available
Carriers and Apple itself are already offering some deals for those who want to pre-order the iPhone Duo this Friday. Apple's trade-in program alone offers up to $885 off, depending on the phone you trade in, which helps offset the full price. Or you can pay in installments with your Apple Card, interest-free, with prices starting at $83.29 per month for 24 months on the base model. There's also Apple Upgrade, a financing program in partnership with Klarna, with prices starting at $57.99 per month for 24 months. At the end of the contract, you can either return the device, pay off the remaining balance or upgrade to a new iPhone.
Carriers are also going big on deals for the iPhone Duo, with AT&T offering up to $1,200 in trade-in credit for eligible devices. T-Mobile, on the other hand, offers up to $1,000 in trade-in credit for Xfinity Mobile Plus customers. Even if you don't trade in your old phone, Mobile Plus customers can get a $400 discount when pre-ordering an iPhone Duo. With prices exceeding $2,000, any discount is more than welcome.
Accessories worth considering
People love buying accessories for their new phones, and it won't be any different with the iPhone Duo. Apple has introduced its own range of new accessories designed specifically for its first foldable phone, and you prefer a first-party option. The company's iPhone Duo Case costs $79 and covers all sides of the phone. The case is made of plastic and is ideal for those looking for better protection against accidental drops. It's only available in two colors, though: Navy Blue and Sand, to match the blue and silver iPhones.
Also from Apple is the Duo Folio case, which features a built-in kickstand on the back. This cover is much more elegant and attaches magnetically to the iPhone, making it much thinner and easier to put on and take off. It costs $129 and...
